titulo: How Many Trading Days Are There in 2026, and Why It Matters
descricao: The US market has 251 trading days in 2026. See how to use that number to plan more realistic monthly goals.
corpo:
Many traders set annual goals without ever stopping to count how many real chances to trade exist in that year. In 2026, the US stock market has 251 trading days, one less than the more common 252 days, because of how holidays and weekends fall on the calendar.

Knowing this number, and how it's distributed across the months, helps plan goals more realistically, instead of treating every month of the year as if they were identical.

The total isn't the same across every market

Not every market follows exactly the same calendar. According to the data behind this article, in 2026:

  • US stocks and options have 251 trading days.
  • Interest rate products have 257 sessions, a higher number because some of these markets trade on days when the stock exchange is closed.
  • Commodities and currencies generally follow the same 251-day total as stocks.

February is the shortest month

According to the same data, February 2026 has just 19 trading days for stocks, the shortest month of the year. March, July, October, and December, on the other hand, appear as the longest months, with 22 trading days each.

This difference has a practical psychological effect: in shorter months, it's common to feel more pressure to make up for lost time, which can lead to rushed decisions. Knowing in advance that February is naturally shorter helps adjust result expectations for that month, without forcing trades just to hit an arbitrary goal.

Holidays that close the US market in 2026

According to the 2026 calendar, full market closure days in the US include, among others, New Year's Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Presidents' Day, Good Friday, Memorial Day, Independence Day (observed on a Friday, since July 4 falls on a Saturday), Labor Day, Thanksgiving, and Christmas.

Besides full holidays, there are early-close days, when the market closes earlier than usual, usually the day before Thanksgiving, the day after it (the so-called Black Friday), and Christmas Eve. These days tend to have lower volume and less reliable moves, which leads many more experienced traders to reduce position size or simply not trade during those sessions.

How to use this calendar in planning

Instead of splitting an annual goal equally across twelve months, it makes more sense to adjust monthly expectations by taking into account the actual number of trading days available:

  • Longer months, like March and December, allow more time to recover from any losing streaks.
  • Shorter months, like February, call for proportionally smaller goals, and more patience to avoid forcing trades.
  • Weeks with a holiday in the middle tend to behave differently: they can get slower before a holiday, or busier right after, when the market reacts to news that built up during the holiday.

A detail for those trading international markets

If you trade international assets or currency pairs on Duotide, it's worth remembering that the US calendar is just one reference among several. Other countries have their own holidays and even fiscal years that don't match the calendar year: the United Kingdom, for example, uses a fiscal year that runs from April to March, and Australia's runs from July to June. This can affect the liquidity of certain assets even on days when the US market is operating normally.

In practice

Before locking in your goals for the year, it's worth marking on the calendar the holidays and early-close days of the market you trade most, and adjusting monthly expectations according to the actual number of sessions available. This simple adjustment reduces the pressure to try to make up for lost time in naturally shorter months, which by itself helps maintain discipline in risk management throughout the year.

It's also worth reviewing the calendar at the start of each quarter, not just once at the beginning of the year. Adjusting quarterly goals according to the actual number of trading days remaining tends to generate more realistic expectations than a fixed annual goal, distributed evenly without accounting for the differences between months.
